claim: Piezo1 mRNA is highly expressed in mouse ileal mucosa.
source: Piezo1 mRNA was found to be highly expressed in both mouse ileal mucosa and STC-1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A measuring mRNA levels.

claim: Piezo1 mRNA is highly expressed in STC-1 cells.
source: Piezo1 mRNA was found to be highly expressed in both mouse ileal mucosa and STC-1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A measuring mRNA levels.

claim: Piezo1 is co-localized with GLP-1 in mouse ileal sections from NCD fed mice.
source: Moreover, Piezo1 was co-localized with GLP-1 in immunofluorescent staining on NCD fed mouse ileal sections, indicating its expression in L cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Piezo1 is expressed in intestinal L cells.
source: Moreover, Piezo1 was co-localized with GLP-1 in immunofluorescent staining on NCD fed mouse ileal sections, indicating its expression in L cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from co-localization data with GLP-1, a marker of L cells.

claim: High-fat diet-induced diabetic mice exhibit increased body weight compared to normal chow diet fed mice.
source: Interestingly, increased body weight and impaired glucose tolerance were observed in high-fat diet-induced diabetic mice, while Piezo1 and Proglucagon expression levels in the ileal mucosa of diabetic mice were significantly lower than that in mice feed with normal chow diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: High-fat diet-induced diabetic mice exhibit impaired glucose tolerance compared to normal chow diet fed mice.
source: Interestingly, increased body weight and impaired glucose tolerance were observed in high-fat diet-induced diabetic mice, while Piezo1 and Proglucagon expression levels in the ileal mucosa of diabetic mice were significantly lower than that in mice feed with normal chow diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Piezo1 expression levels in the ileal mucosa of high-fat diet-induced diabetic mice are significantly lower than in mice fed with normal chow diet.
source: Interestingly, increased body weight and impaired glucose tolerance were observed in high-fat diet-induced diabetic mice, while Piezo1 and Proglucagon expression levels in the ileal mucosa of diabetic mice were significantly lower than that in mice feed with normal chow diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by mRNA and protein expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Proglucagon expression levels in the ileal mucosa of high-fat diet-induced diabetic mice are significantly lower than in mice fed with normal chow diet.
source: Interestingly, increased body weight and impaired glucose tolerance were observed in high-fat diet-induced diabetic mice, while Piezo1 and Proglucagon expression levels in the ileal mucosa of diabetic mice were significantly lower than that in mice feed with normal chow diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Ileal mucosal Piezo1 mRNA levels are positively correlated with Gcg mRNA levels.
source: Moreover, ileal mucosal Piezo1 mRNA levels were positively correlated with Gcg mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), but negatively correlated with the AUC of glucose tolerance test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Ileal mucosal Piezo1 mRNA levels are negatively correlated with the AUC of glucose tolerance test.
source: Moreover, ileal mucosal Piezo1 mRNA levels were positively correlated with Gcg mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), but negatively correlated with the AUC of glucose tolerance test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Obese T2DM patients who underwent RYGB surgery showed decreased BMI compared to before surgery.
source: Obese T2DM patients who underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery showed decreased BMI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and increased Piezo1 and GLP-1 in ileal mucosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J, K) compared to that before surgery.
evidence: Supported by BMI measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Obese T2DM patients who underwent RYGB surgery showed increased Piezo1 in ileal mucosa compared to before surgery.
source: Obese T2DM patients who underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery showed decreased BMI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and increased Piezo1 and GLP-1 in ileal mucosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J, K) compared to that before surgery.
evidence: Supported by mRNA and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J-K.

claim: Obese T2DM patients who underwent RYGB surgery showed increased GLP-1 in ileal mucosa compared to before surgery.
source: Obese T2DM patients who underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery showed decreased BMI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and increased Piezo1 and GLP-1 in ileal mucosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J, K) compared to that before surgery.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Piezo1 level varies in different energy status.
source: These findings indicated that Piezo1 is expressed in intestinal L cells and its level varies in different energy status.
evidence: Inferred from the differences in Piezo1 expression between NCD and HFD mice, and before and after RYGB surgery.

claim: Proglucagon is mainly expressed in both L cells and pancreatic α cells.
source: Proglucagon (encoded by Gcg gene) is mainly expressed in both L cells and pancreatic α cells (Jin, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jin, 2008.

claim: Villin-1 is expressed in gastrointestinal epithelium, including L cells.
source: Villin-1 (encoded by Vil1 gene) is expressed in gastrointestinal epithelium, including L cells, but not in pancreatic α cells (Maunoury et al., 1992; Rutlin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maunoury et al., 1992 and Rutlin et al., 2020.

claim: Villin-1 is not expressed in pancreatic α cells.
source: Villin-1 (encoded by Vil1 gene) is expressed in gastrointestinal epithelium, including L cells, but not in pancreatic α cells (Maunoury et al., 1992; Rutlin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maunoury et al., 1992 and Rutlin et al., 2020.

claim: Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice enable L-cell-specific Cre expression.
source: We further crossed the Vil1FLP mice with GcgCre mice to obtain L-cell-specific Cre mice (Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre), in which Vil1 promoter-driven Flippase flipped the reverse Cre cassette into a correct orientation in Villin-positive cells (including L cells, but not pancreatic α cells), and thus Cre can only be expressed under the Gcg promoter in L cells.
evidence: Supported by the genetic strategy described and validated by PCR and reporter mice data.

claim: The flipping of the reverse Cre cassette occurred in the intestine but not in the pancreas of Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice.
source: The flipping of the reverse Cre cassette was validated by PCR, which confirmed that the flipping only occurred the intestine, but not in the pancreas (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EGFP expression was only observed scatteredly in the intestine, but not in the pancreas of Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre-Rosa26mT/mG mice.
source: EGFP expression was only observed scatteredly in the intestine, but not in the pancreas, indicating the intestine-specific Cre activity in the Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice have intestine-specific Cre activity.
source: EGFP expression was only observed scatteredly in the intestine, but not in the pancreas, indicating the intestine-specific Cre activity in the Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the EGFP expression pattern in reporter mice.

claim: Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exhibited increased body weight compared to control groups under normal chow diet.
source: Under normal chow diet, Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exhibited increased body weight (Figure 1G) and greater glycemic excursions compared to control groups (Piezo1loxp/loxp, Vil1FLP, GcgCre and Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre; Figure 1H and I), while the food and water intake were not changed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exhibited greater glycemic excursions compared to control groups under normal chow diet.
source: Under normal chow diet, Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exhibited increased body weight (Figure 1G) and greater glycemic excursions compared to control groups (Piezo1loxp/loxp, Vil1FLP, GcgCre and Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre; Figure 1H and I), while the food and water intake were not changed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by IPGTT and ITT data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Food and water intake were not changed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice compared to controls under normal chow diet.
source: Under normal chow diet, Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exhibited increased body weight (Figure 1G) and greater glycemic excursions compared to control groups (Piezo1loxp/loxp, Vil1FLP, GcgCre and Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre; Figure 1H and I), while the food and water intake were not changed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by food and water intake measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The morphology of islet was not affected in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: The morphology of islet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and ileum (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) were not affected.
evidence: Supported by HE staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The morphology of ileum was not affected in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: The morphology of islet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and ileum (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) were not affected.
evidence: Supported by HE staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Ileal mucosal Proglucagon expression was significantly lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice than in all littermate controls.
source: Ileal mucosal Proglucagon expression and plasma GLP-1 level were significantly lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice than that in all littermate controls such as Piezo1loxp/loxp, Vil1FLP, GcgCre and Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice (Figure 1J and K), while no significant alteration was observed in the expression of pancreatic Piezo1 and Proglucagon (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by mRNA measurements shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Plasma GLP-1 level was significantly lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice than in all littermate controls.
source: Ileal mucosal Proglucagon expression and plasma GLP-1 level were significantly lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice than that in all littermate controls such as Piezo1loxp/loxp, Vil1FLP, GcgCre and Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice (Figure 1J and K), while no significant alteration was observed in the expression of pancreatic Piezo1 and Proglucagon (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1K.

claim: No significant alteration was observed in the expression of pancreatic Piezo1 in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Ileal mucosal Proglucagon expression and plasma GLP-1 level were significantly lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice than that in all littermate controls such as Piezo1loxp/loxp, Vil1FLP, GcgCre and Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice (Figure 1J and K), while no significant alteration was observed in the expression of pancreatic Piezo1 and Proglucagon (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by mRNA and protein data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-D.

claim: No significant alteration was observed in the expression of pancreatic Proglucagon in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Ileal mucosal Proglucagon expression and plasma GLP-1 level were significantly lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice than that in all littermate controls such as Piezo1loxp/loxp, Vil1FLP, GcgCre and Vil1FLP::GcgfrtCre mice (Figure 1J and K), while no significant alteration was observed in the expression of pancreatic Piezo1 and Proglucagon (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by mRNA and protein data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-D.

claim: The expression of Piezo1 disappeared in GLP-1 positive cells in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: According to in situ hybridization of Piezo1 and immunofluorescence analysis of GLP-1, the expression of Piezo1 disappeared in GLP-1 positive cells, suggesting successful knockout of Piezo1 in L cells in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: Piezo1 knockout in L cells was successful in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: According to in situ hybridization of Piezo1 and immunofluorescence analysis of GLP-1, the expression of Piezo1 disappeared in GLP-1 positive cells, suggesting successful knockout of Piezo1 in L cells in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: Inferred from the absence of Piezo1 in GLP-1 positive cells.

claim: Piezo1 is expressed in GLP-1-positive cells of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and colon in control mice.
source: Also depicted in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Piezo1 is expressed in GLP-1-positive cells of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and colon in control mice, but not in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Piezo1 is not expressed in GLP-1-positive cells of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and colon in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Also depicted in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Piezo1 is expressed in GLP-1-positive cells of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and colon in control mice, but not in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Piezo1 remains expressed in intestinal ghrelin positive cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: However, Piezo1 remains expressed in intestinal ghrelin positive cells and pancreatic glucagon-positive cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Piezo1 remains expressed in pancreatic glucagon-positive cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: However, Piezo1 remains expressed in intestinal ghrelin positive cells and pancreatic glucagon-positive cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: GLP-1 levels were reduced in L cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Moreover, while GLP-1 levels were reduced in L cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice, levels of PYY, another hormone secreted by L cells, were unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C-D.

claim: Levels of PYY were unaffected in L cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Moreover, while GLP-1 levels were reduced in L cells of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice, levels of PYY, another hormone secreted by L cells, were unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A-B.

claim: Ileal mucosal cholecystokinin (CCK) was unchanged in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Additionally, ileal mucosal cholecystokinin (CCK), a hormone secreted by I cells with metabolic effects similar to GLP-1, was also unchanged in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 7E).
evidence: Supported by mRNA measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7E.

claim: Piezo1 affected intestinal tight junctions and epithelial integrity in a previous study.
source: Previous study showed that Piezo1 affected intestinal tight junctions and epithelial integrity (Jiang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2021.

claim: The expression of ZO-1 remained unchanged in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice when compared to littermate controls.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8, the expression of ZO-1 and Occludin remained unchanged in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice when compared to littermate controls.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The expression of Occludin remained unchanged in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice when compared to littermate controls.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8, the expression of ZO-1 and Occludin remained unchanged in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice when compared to littermate controls.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Piezo1 is a non-selective cationic channel that allows passage of Ca2+ and Na+.
source: Piezo1 is a non-selective cationic channel that allows passage of Ca2+ and Na+.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Piezo1 channel properties.

claim: CaMKKβ is the main calcium/calmodulin dependent protein kinase kinase involved in the regulation of metabolic homeostasis.
source: CaMKKβ is the main calcium/calmodulin dependent protein kinase kinase involved in the regulation of metabolic homeostasis (Marcelo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marcelo et al., 2016.

claim: CaMKKβ is activated by binding calcium-calmodulin (Ca2+/CaM), resulting in downstream activation of kinases CaMKIV.
source: It is activated by binding calcium-calmodulin (Ca2+/CaM), resulting in downstream activation of kinases CaMKIV.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of CaMKKβ signaling pathway.

claim: The activation of CaMKIV modulates the gene expression of nutrient- and hormone-related proteins.
source: The activation of CaMKIV modulate the gene expression of nutrient- and hormone-related proteins (Ban et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2011; Takemoto-Kimura et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ban et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2011; Takemoto-Kimura et al., 2017.

claim: Ca2+ and mTOR signaling regulate the production of GLP-1.
source: Previous studies have reported that Ca2+ and mTOR signaling regulate the production of GLP-1 (Tolhurst et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2015; Yu and Jin, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tolhurst et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2015; Yu and Jin, 2010.

claim: Piezo1 may regulate GLP-1 synthesis via the CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling pathway.
source: Drawing from these findings, this research study proposed a hypothesis that Piezo1 may regulate GLP-1 synthesis via the CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling pathway (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on inference from previous findings and the properties of Piezo1.

claim: Abrogated GLP-1 production was associated with decreased CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling in the ileal mucosa of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: As shown in Figure 1O, abrogated GLP-1 production was associated with decreased CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling in the ileal mucosa of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 1O).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1O.

claim: Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD exhibited higher body weight compared to controls.
source: Compared to the controls, higher body weight (Figure 2A), greater glucose excursions (Figure 2B) were observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD.
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD exhibited greater glucose excursions compared to controls.
source: Compared to the controls, higher body weight (Figure 2A), greater glucose excursions (Figure 2B) were observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD.
evidence: Supported by IPGTT data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ileal mucosal Proglucagon expression levels were lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD than control mice.
source: Ileal mucosal Proglucagon expression levels were lower in Piezo1 IntL-CKO than control mice (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by mRNA, immunofluorescence, and western blot data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Impaired CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling pathway in ileal mucosa was observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD.
source: Impaired CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling pathway in ileal mucosa as evidenced by a decrease in CaMKKβ, reduced phosphorylation levels of CaMKIV, mTOR, S6K, and S6 was also observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No significant alteration in morphology of the pancreas was observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD.
source: No significant alteration in morphology, Piezo1 or Proglucagon levels were observed in the pancreas of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by HE staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant alteration in Piezo1 levels were observed in the pancreas of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD.
source: No significant alteration in morphology, Piezo1 or Proglucagon levels were observed in the pancreas of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by mRNA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant alteration in Proglucagon levels were observed in the pancreas of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice exposed to HFD.
source: No significant alteration in morphology, Piezo1 or Proglucagon levels were observed in the pancreas of Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by mRNA and western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice with prolonged HFD feeding exhibit impaired glucose metabolism phenotype and reduced GLP-1.
source: Together these data demonstrate that Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice with prolonged HFD feeding exhibit impaired glucose metabolism phenotype and reduced GLP-1.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data on body weight, glucose tolerance, and GLP-1 levels.

claim: Injection of GLP-1 analog Exendin-4 (Ex-4) decreased the body weight in control and Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Injection of GLP-1 analog Exendin-4 (Ex-4) decreased the body weight (Figure 2G) and improved both glucose tolerance (Figure 2H) and insulin resistance (Figure 2I) in control and Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice, while endogenous synthesis of GLP-1 was not changed by Ex-4 injection in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Injection of GLP-1 analog Exendin-4 (Ex-4) improved glucose tolerance in control and Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Injection of GLP-1 analog Exendin-4 (Ex-4) decreased the body weight (Figure 2G) and improved both glucose tolerance (Figure 2H) and insulin resistance (Figure 2I) in control and Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice, while endogenous synthesis of GLP-1 was not changed by Ex-4 injection in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: Supported by IPGTT data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Injection of GLP-1 analog Exendin-4 (Ex-4) improved insulin resistance in control and Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Injection of GLP-1 analog Exendin-4 (Ex-4) decreased the body weight (Figure 2G) and improved both glucose tolerance (Figure 2H) and insulin resistance (Figure 2I) in control and Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice, while endogenous synthesis of GLP-1 was not changed by Ex-4 injection in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: Supported by ITT data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Endogenous synthesis of GLP-1 was not changed by Ex-4 injection in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: Injection of GLP-1 analog Exendin-4 (Ex-4) decreased the body weight (Figure 2G) and improved both glucose tolerance (Figure 2H) and insulin resistance (Figure 2I) in control and Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice, while endogenous synthesis of GLP-1 was not changed by Ex-4 injection in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: Supported by mRNA and ELISA data shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: Decreased GLP-1 synthesis and secretion contribute to impaired glucose metabolism in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: These data suggested that decreased GLP-1 synthesis and secretion contribute to impaired glucose metabolism in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of glucose metabolism by exogenous GLP-1 analog.

claim: Injection of Piezo1 activator Yoda1 led to reduced body weight in diabetic mice.
source: Injection of Piezo1 activator Yoda1 after 10 weeks of high-fat diet, led to reduced body weight and improved the impaired glucose metabolism significantly in diabetic mice, while Piezo1 antagonist GsMTx4 reversed the weight loss and glucose-lowering effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Injection of Piezo1 activator Yoda1 improved the impaired glucose metabolism significantly in diabetic mice.
source: Injection of Piezo1 activator Yoda1 after 10 weeks of high-fat diet, led to reduced body weight and improved the impaired glucose metabolism significantly in diabetic mice, while Piezo1 antagonist GsMTx4 reversed the weight loss and glucose-lowering effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by IPGTT data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Piezo1 antagonist GsMTx4 reversed the weight loss effect of Yoda1 in diabetic mice.
source: Injection of Piezo1 activator Yoda1 after 10 weeks of high-fat diet, led to reduced body weight and improved the impaired glucose metabolism significantly in diabetic mice, while Piezo1 antagonist GsMTx4 reversed the weight loss and glucose-lowering effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Piezo1 antagonist GsMTx4 reversed the glucose-lowering effect of Yoda1 in diabetic mice.
source: Injection of Piezo1 activator Yoda1 after 10 weeks of high-fat diet, led to reduced body weight and improved the impaired glucose metabolism significantly in diabetic mice, while Piezo1 antagonist GsMTx4 reversed the weight loss and glucose-lowering effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by IPGTT data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Yoda1 remarkably induced an increase in GLP-1 synthesis and secretion in diabetic mice.
source: Yoda1 remarkably induced an increase in GLP-1 synthesis and secretion (Figure 3C and D), as well as an increment of CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling in ileal mucosa (Figure 3E), while GsMTx4 abolished the effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by mRNA and ELISA data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Yoda1 induced an increment of CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling in ileal mucosa of diabetic mice.
source: Yoda1 remarkably induced an increase in GLP-1 synthesis and secretion (Figure 3C and D), as well as an increment of CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling in ileal mucosa (Figure 3E), while GsMTx4 abolished the effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GsMTx4 abolished the effect of Yoda1 on GLP-1 synthesis and secretion in diabetic mice.
source: Yoda1 remarkably induced an increase in GLP-1 synthesis and secretion (Figure 3C and D), as well as an increment of CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling in ileal mucosa (Figure 3E), while GsMTx4 abolished the effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by mRNA and ELISA data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: GsMTx4 abolished the effect of Yoda1 on CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling in ileal mucosa of diabetic mice.
source: Yoda1 remarkably induced an increase in GLP-1 synthesis and secretion (Figure 3C and D), as well as an increment of CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTORC1 signaling in ileal mucosa (Figure 3E), while GsMTx4 abolished the effect of Yoda1 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Weight loss induced by Yoda1 was not observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: However, weight loss, improved plasma glucose and increased GLP-1 production induced by Yoda1 were not observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Improved plasma glucose induced by Yoda1 was not observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: However, weight loss, improved plasma glucose and increased GLP-1 production induced by Yoda1 were not observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Supported by fasting blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Increased GLP-1 production induced by Yoda1 was not observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice.
source: However, weight loss, improved plasma glucose and increased GLP-1 production induced by Yoda1 were not observed in Piezo1 IntL-CKO mice (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Supported by mRNA, ELISA, and western blot data shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: Intestinal bead implantation improved the impaired glucose metabolism in diabetic mice.
source: Intestinal bead implantation improved the impaired glucose metabolism in diabetic mice (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: Supported by fasting blood glucose and IPGTT data shown in Figure 3K and L.

claim: Body weight loss was observed in diabetic mice after intestinal bead implantation.
source: Body weight loss, activated ileal mucosal CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling, increased mRNA and protein levels of ileal mucosal Piezo1 and Proglucagon, as well as the circulating levels of GLP-1 were observed in diabetic mice after operation (Figure 3M–R).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Activated ileal mucosal CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling was observed in diabetic mice after intestinal bead implantation.
source: Body weight loss, activated ileal mucosal CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling, increased mRNA and protein levels of ileal mucosal Piezo1 and Proglucagon, as well as the circulating levels of GLP-1 were observed in diabetic mice after operation (Figure 3M–R).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3R.

claim: Increased mRNA and protein levels of ileal mucosal Piezo1 were observed in diabetic mice after intestinal bead implantation.
source: Body weight loss, activated ileal mucosal CaMKKβ/CaMKIV-mTOR signaling, increased mRNA and protein levels of ileal mucosal Piezo1 and Proglucagon, as well as the circulating levels of GLP-1 were observed in diabetic mice after operation (Figure 3M–R).
